Applied Example: Estimating reliability of reinforcement learning parameters using data from Pike et al 2026

Author

Giacomo Bignardi

Claude Code was used to prepare the first draft of this document, which was later checked and edited.

Background

All data from this script comes from Pike, A. C., … Roiser, J. P. (2026). The recoverability, reliability, and generalizability of reward processing parameters and relation to mental health symptoms. Psychological Medicine, 56, e238. doi:10.1017/S0033291726105340.

The models and datasets are available on the Open Science Framework. To download the models, you may need to press the “Models” tab in Files Preview.

We use data from the Fluctuating Bandit task (task A).

Rather than using the custom Stan model that the authors used, this notebook uses the bandit4arm_4par() function from hBayesDM. This is a hierarchical Bayesian implementation of the 4-parameter model from Seymour, Daw, Roiser, Dayan, & Dolan (2012), which is run using a cmdstanr backend. The Stan code for the bandit4arm_4par() model is printed in full in the appendix below, alongside a walkthrough of how it works.

Setup

Analyses are run inside the bignardig/tidyverse461:v5 Docker container - which includes all dependencies except the cmdstan install (v2.39.0).

The script 02_01_pike_2026_fit_bandit_models.R fits the main Bayesian models to time 1 and time 2 separately. It models only the N = 115 subjects who completed both sessions (the matched test-retest subsample, not the full N = 547 sample).

The script 02_01_pike_2026_fit_bandit_splithalf_models.R fits the Bayesian models four times, splitting the data at each timepoint into halves to estimate split-half reliability at each time point. It models only the N = 115 subjects who completed both sessions.

The script 02_01_pike_2026_fit_bandit_fullsample.R fits the Bayesian model to the full (N = 547) dataset and also to split-half datasets to estimate RMU and split-half reliability on the full sample.

Run the three fitting scripts once, in order, before rendering this notebook (from the applied_example_pike/ directory, e.g. inside the bignardig/tidyverse461:v5 container):

Rscript 02_01_pike_2026_fit_bandit_models.R
Rscript 02_01_pike_2026_fit_bandit_splithalf_models.R
Rscript 02_01_pike_2026_fit_bandit_fullsample.R
rm(list = ls())
library(gbtoolbox)
library(hBayesDM)
library(cmdstanr)
library(bayesplot)
library(tidyverse)
library(gt)

data_dir = file.path("data", "pike_2026")
subj_pars = c("Arew", "Apun", "R", "P")
hyper_pars = c("mu_pr", "sigma")

Data

A look at the raw data files behind this notebook

Raw trial-level exports

bandit.csv / bandit2.csv are the authors’ raw per-trial exports for session 1 / session 2 (one row per trial). I’ve filtered down to the columns actually used for modelling.

setwd("..") # set the working directory to the parent folder which has /data/

bandit_model_cols = c("id", "trial_nr", "is_gain", "is_loss", "response")

bandit_raw_t1 = read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "bandit.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  select(all_of(bandit_model_cols))
bandit_raw_t2 = read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "bandit2.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  select(all_of(bandit_model_cols))

Time 1

rmarkdown::paged_table(bandit_raw_t1, options = list(rows.print = 25, cols.print = ncol(bandit_raw_t1)))

Time 2

rmarkdown::paged_table(bandit_raw_t2, options = list(rows.print = 25, cols.print = ncol(bandit_raw_t2)))

hBayesDM-ready data frames

hBayesDM::bandit4arm_4par() expects one row per trial, with columns subjID/choice/gain/loss. bandit4arm_df() (data/pike_2026/utils.R) builds that row-per-trial data.frame directly from the raw csvs above, for the matched N = 115 subjects that 02_01_pike_2026_fit_bandit_models.R fits.

setwd("..") # set the working directory to the parent folder which has /data/

source(file.path(data_dir, "utils.R")) # provides bandit4arm_df()

bandit4arm_df
function (data, ids = NULL) 
{
    if (!is.null(ids)) 
        data <- data %>% filter(id %in% ids)
    data %>% arrange(id, trial_nr) %>% group_by(id, trial_nr) %>% 
        slice_tail(n = 1) %>% ungroup() %>% transmute(subjID = id, 
        choice = response, gain = is_gain, loss = is_loss)
}
ids_t2_preview = bandit_raw_t2 %>% distinct(id) %>% arrange(id) %>% pull(id)
ids_t1_preview = bandit_raw_t1 %>% filter(id %in% ids_t2_preview) %>% distinct(id) %>% arrange(id) %>% pull(id)

bandit_df_t1 = bandit4arm_df(bandit_raw_t1, ids_t1_preview)
bandit_df_t2 = bandit4arm_df(bandit_raw_t2, ids_t2_preview)

rmarkdown::paged_table(bandit_df_t1, options = list(rows.print = 25, cols.print = ncol(bandit_df_t1)))

setwd("..") # set the working directory to the parent folder which has /data/

fits_dir = file.path(data_dir, "model_fits")

if (!file.exists(file.path(fits_dir, "fit_bandit4arm4par_t1.RDS"))) {
  stop("No saved fits found. Run 02_01_pike_2026_fit_bandit_models.R first.")
}
if (!file.exists(file.path(fits_dir, "fit_bandit4arm4par_fullsample.RDS"))) {
  stop("No full-sample fit found. Run 02_01_pike_2026_fit_bandit_fullsample.R first.")
}
if (!file.exists(file.path(fits_dir, "fit_bandit4arm4par_t1_first.RDS"))) {
  stop("No split-half fits found. Run 02_01_pike_2026_fit_bandit_splithalf_models.R first.")
}
if (!file.exists(file.path(fits_dir, "fit_bandit4arm4par_fullsample_first.RDS"))) {
  stop("No full-sample split-half fits found. Run 02_01_pike_2026_fit_bandit_fullsample.R first.")
}

# retest sample (N = 115), time 1 / time 2
ids_t1 = readRDS(file.path(fits_dir, "bandit_ids_t1t2.RDS"))
ids_t2 = ids_t1 # same 115 subjects, same order -- enforced when the fit data.frames were built

fit_bandit_t1 = readRDS(file.path(fits_dir, "fit_bandit4arm4par_t1.RDS"))
fit_bandit_t2 = readRDS(file.path(fits_dir, "fit_bandit4arm4par_t2.RDS"))

# full T1 sample (N = 547)
ids_all = readRDS(file.path(fits_dir, "bandit_ids_all.RDS"))
fit_bandit_all = readRDS(file.path(fits_dir, "fit_bandit4arm4par_fullsample.RDS"))

# retest sample split-half (N = 115), time 1 / time 2
ids_splithalf = readRDS(file.path(fits_dir, "bandit_splithalf_ids.RDS"))

fit_bandit_t1_first  = readRDS(file.path(fits_dir, "fit_bandit4arm4par_t1_first.RDS"))
fit_bandit_t1_second = readRDS(file.path(fits_dir, "fit_bandit4arm4par_t1_second.RDS"))
fit_bandit_t2_first  = readRDS(file.path(fits_dir, "fit_bandit4arm4par_t2_first.RDS"))
fit_bandit_t2_second = readRDS(file.path(fits_dir, "fit_bandit4arm4par_t2_second.RDS"))

# full T1 sample split-half (N = 547)
fit_bandit_fullsample_first  = readRDS(file.path(fits_dir, "fit_bandit4arm4par_fullsample_first.RDS"))
fit_bandit_fullsample_second = readRDS(file.path(fits_dir, "fit_bandit4arm4par_fullsample_second.RDS"))

Diagnostics

We fit bandit4arm_4par() nine times across this notebook – the T1/T2 retest-sample fits, the full T1 sample, and split-half fits for each of those three – so before trusting any of the reliability estimates below, we check convergence across all nine, not just the two headline T1/T2 fits.

all_fits = list(
  "T1 (retest, N = 115)"          = fit_bandit_t1,
  "T2 (retest, N = 115)"          = fit_bandit_t2,
  "Full T1 sample (N = 547)"      = fit_bandit_all,
  "T1 first-half (N = 115)"       = fit_bandit_t1_first,
  "T1 second-half (N = 115)"      = fit_bandit_t1_second,
  "T2 first-half (N = 115)"       = fit_bandit_t2_first,
  "T2 second-half (N = 115)"      = fit_bandit_t2_second,
  "Full T1 first-half (N = 547)"  = fit_bandit_fullsample_first,
  "Full T1 second-half (N = 547)" = fit_bandit_fullsample_second
)

diag_pars  = c(hyper_pars, subj_pars)

rhat_threshold = 1.01
ess_threshold  = 400 # cmdstanr's own rule of thumb: bulk/tail ESS < 100 per chain (400 across our 4 chains)

Sampler diagnostics (divergences, treedepth, E-BFMI)

sampler_diag = imap_dfr(all_fits, function(fit, label) {
  d = fit$diagnostic_summary()
  tibble(
    model           = label,
    n_divergent     = sum(d$num_divergent),
    n_max_treedepth = sum(d$num_max_treedepth),
    min_ebfmi       = min(d$ebfmi)
  )
})

sampler_diag %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(columns = min_ebfmi, decimals = 2) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = list(cell_fill(color = "#f8d7da"), cell_text(weight = "bold")),
    locations = cells_body(columns = n_divergent, rows = n_divergent > 0)
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = list(cell_fill(color = "#f8d7da"), cell_text(weight = "bold")),
    locations = cells_body(columns = n_max_treedepth, rows = n_max_treedepth > 0)
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = list(cell_fill(color = "#f8d7da"), cell_text(weight = "bold")),
    locations = cells_body(columns = min_ebfmi, rows = min_ebfmi < 0.3)
  )

Rhat / ESS by parameter, across all models

Rather than eyeballing summary() output fit-by-fit, we collapse each fit’s per-subject rhat/ess_bulk/ess_tail down to one row per parameter family (mu_pr, sigma, Arew, Apun, R, P) – taking the worst (max rhat / min ESS) across subjects within that family – so a single bad subject-level parameter can’t hide inside a fit-wide average. Flagged cells breach the conventional rhat > 1.01 / ESS < 400 thresholds.

param_diag = imap_dfr(all_fits, function(fit, label) {
  fit$summary(variables = diag_pars) %>%
    mutate(parameter = str_extract(variable, "^[^\\[]+")) %>%
    group_by(parameter) %>%
    summarise(
      max_rhat     = max(rhat, na.rm = TRUE),
      min_ess_bulk = min(ess_bulk, na.rm = TRUE),
      min_ess_tail = min(ess_tail, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    mutate(model = label, .before = 1)
}) %>%
  mutate(parameter = factor(parameter, levels = diag_pars))

param_diag %>%
  gt(groupname_col = "model") %>%
  fmt_number(columns = max_rhat, decimals = 3) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = c(min_ess_bulk, min_ess_tail), decimals = 0) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = list(cell_fill(color = "#f8d7da"), cell_text(weight = "bold")),
    locations = cells_body(columns = max_rhat, rows = max_rhat > rhat_threshold)
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = list(cell_fill(color = "#f8d7da"), cell_text(weight = "bold")),
    locations = cells_body(columns = min_ess_bulk, rows = min_ess_bulk < ess_threshold)
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = list(cell_fill(color = "#f8d7da"), cell_text(weight = "bold")),
    locations = cells_body(columns = min_ess_tail, rows = min_ess_tail < ess_threshold)
  )

Parameters with consistently poor convergence

Collapsing the table above across models: for each parameter family, the worst rhat/ESS seen in any of the nine fits, which fit produced it, and how many fits flag it – so a parameter that’s borderline everywhere is distinguishable from one bad fit dragging down an otherwise clean parameter.

param_summary = param_diag %>%
  group_by(parameter) %>%
  summarise(
    worst_rhat            = max(max_rhat),
    worst_rhat_model       = model[which.max(max_rhat)],
    worst_ess_bulk         = min(min_ess_bulk),
    worst_ess_bulk_model   = model[which.min(min_ess_bulk)],
    n_models_rhat_flagged = sum(max_rhat > rhat_threshold),
    n_models_ess_flagged  = sum(min_ess_bulk < ess_threshold),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(worst_rhat))

param_summary %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(columns = worst_rhat, decimals = 3) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = worst_ess_bulk, decimals = 0) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = list(cell_fill(color = "#f8d7da"), cell_text(weight = "bold")),
    locations = cells_body(columns = n_models_rhat_flagged, rows = n_models_rhat_flagged > 0)
  ) %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = list(cell_fill(color = "#f8d7da"), cell_text(weight = "bold")),
    locations = cells_body(columns = n_models_ess_flagged, rows = n_models_ess_flagged > 0)
  )

Subject-level checks

The per-parameter table above takes the worst subject in each fit – it can’t tell us whether the same handful of subjects are consistently unidentifiable (worth flagging, or excluding, individually) or whether the problem is spread thinly across many different subjects (more likely a sampler-tuning issue than a subject-data issue). We rebuild the same rhat/ESS check but keep every subject, then rank subjects by how often they’re flagged across all the (fit x parameter) combinations they appear in.

all_ids = list(
  "T1 (retest, N = 115)"          = ids_t1,
  "T2 (retest, N = 115)"          = ids_t2,
  "Full T1 sample (N = 547)"      = ids_all,
  "T1 first-half (N = 115)"       = ids_splithalf,
  "T1 second-half (N = 115)"      = ids_splithalf,
  "T2 first-half (N = 115)"       = ids_splithalf,
  "T2 second-half (N = 115)"      = ids_splithalf,
  "Full T1 first-half (N = 547)"  = ids_all,
  "Full T1 second-half (N = 547)" = ids_all
)

subject_diag = imap_dfr(all_fits, function(fit, label) {
  ids = all_ids[[label]]
  fit$summary(variables = subj_pars) %>%
    mutate(
      parameter = str_extract(variable, "^[^\\[]+"),
      idx       = as.integer(str_extract(variable, "(?<=\\[)\\d+(?=\\])")),
      id        = ids[idx]
    ) %>%
    select(id, parameter, rhat, ess_bulk, ess_tail) %>%
    mutate(model = label, .before = 1)
}) %>%
  mutate(
    parameter = factor(parameter, levels = subj_pars),
    flagged   = rhat > rhat_threshold | ess_bulk < ess_threshold
  )

subject_flag_summary = subject_diag %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  summarise(
    n_evaluated    = n(), # how many (fit x parameter) combinations this subject appears in
    n_flagged      = sum(flagged),
    pct_flagged    = n_flagged / n_evaluated,
    worst_rhat     = max(rhat),
    worst_ess_bulk = min(ess_bulk),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(pct_flagged), desc(worst_rhat))

subject_flag_summary %>%
  slice_head(n = 20) %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_percent(columns = pct_flagged, decimals = 0) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = worst_rhat, decimals = 3) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = worst_ess_bulk, decimals = 0) %>%
  tab_header(title = "20 subjects flagged most often (rhat > 1.01 or ESS < 400)") %>%
  tab_style(
    style     = list(cell_fill(color = "#f8d7da"), cell_text(weight = "bold")),
    locations = cells_body(columns = pct_flagged, rows = pct_flagged > 0.5)
  )

If the same subject IDs sit at the top of this table across most rows, that points to specific subjects (e.g. near-random responders where learning rates/sensitivities are only weakly identified by the likelihood) rather than a broad sampler problem. The histogram below shows whether flagged subjects are a small concentrated group or spread across the sample:

subject_flag_summary %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = pct_flagged)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.1, boundary = 0, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(
    x = "Proportion of (fit x parameter) combinations flagged",
    y = "Number of subjects",
    title = "How concentrated is the convergence problem?",
    subtitle = paste0(
      sum(subject_flag_summary$pct_flagged > 0.5), " of ", nrow(subject_flag_summary),
      " subjects are flagged in more than half of the fits/parameters they appear in"
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Group-level parameter trace plots (T1 / T2 retest fits)

mu_pr/sigma are the population mean/SD (probit scale) behind Arew/Apun/R/P, in that order – i.e. mu_pr[2]/sigma[2] are what determine where Apun gets pulled to and how tightly (see the per-subject posterior density discussion below).

mcmc_trace(fit_bandit_t1$draws(variables = hyper_pars))
mcmc_trace(fit_bandit_t2$draws(variables = hyper_pars))

Inspect subject-level parameter estimates

Posterior means

In this section, we extract posterior mean estimates for each subject’s reward learning rate (Arew), punishment learning rate (Apun), reward sensitivity (R) and punishment sensitivity (P).

extract_indpars = function(fit, ids, pars = subj_pars) {
  fit$summary(variables = pars) %>% # This gives a long dataframe with the posterior mean/median/quantiles for each parameter in the model
    mutate(
      parameter = str_extract(variable, "^[^\\[]+"),
      idx       = as.integer(str_extract(variable, "(?<=\\[)\\d+(?=\\])")),
      id        = ids[idx]
    ) %>%
    select(id, parameter, mean, sd) %>%
    pivot_wider(id_cols = id, names_from = parameter, values_from = mean)
}

indpars_t1 = extract_indpars(fit_bandit_t1, ids_t1)
indpars_t2 = extract_indpars(fit_bandit_t2, ids_t2)

Posterior densities

Below we show the posterior densities for each subject, separately for each time point.

get_draws_long = function(fit, ids, pars = subj_pars) {
  fit$draws(variables = pars, format = "df") %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    select(-.chain, -.iteration, -.draw) %>%
    pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
    mutate(
      parameter = str_extract(variable, "^[^\\[]+"),
      idx       = as.integer(str_extract(variable, "(?<=\\[)\\d+(?=\\])")),
      id        = ids[idx]
    )
}

plot_subject_densities = function(fit, ids, session_label, pars = subj_pars, ymax_cap = 20) {
  # browser()
  draws_long = get_draws_long(fit, ids, pars)

  # per-facet y upper limit: each subject's own density peak, capped at ymax_cap
  y_scales = draws_long %>%
    group_by(parameter, id) %>%
    summarise(peak = max(density(value)$y), .groups = "drop") %>%
    group_by(parameter) %>%
    summarise(ymax = min(max(peak), ymax_cap), .groups = "drop") %>%
    arrange(parameter) %>%
    pull(ymax) %>%
    purrr::map(~ scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, .x)))

  draws_long %>%
    ggplot(aes(
      x = value,
      # y = after_stat(scaled),
      group = id)
      ) +
    geom_density(alpha = 0.1, linewidth = 0.3, color = "steelblue") +
    facet_wrap(~parameter, scales = "free") +
    ggh4x::facetted_pos_scales(y = y_scales) +
    labs(
      title = paste0("Per-subject posterior densities — ", session_label),
      subtitle = "One density curve per subject, each scaled to its own peak",
      x = NULL, y = "Density (scaled to subject's peak)"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
}

plot_subject_densities(fit_bandit_t1, ids_t1, "T1")
plot_subject_densities(fit_bandit_t2, ids_t2, "T2")

Test-retest reliability

Correlate each subject’s posterior-mean parameter estimate across the two sessions.

stopifnot(identical(indpars_t1$id, indpars_t2$id))

testretest = map_dfr(subj_pars, function(p) {
  ct = cor.test(indpars_t1[[p]], indpars_t2[[p]])
  r  = unname(ct$estimate)
  tibble(
    parameter = p,
    method    = "Test-Retest (N = 115)",
    estimate  = r,
    se        = sqrt((1 - r^2) / ct$parameter), # SE of Pearson r implied by the t-test df (matches cor.test's statistic)
    lower     = ct$conf.int[1],
    upper     = ct$conf.int[2],
    width     = ct$conf.int[2] - ct$conf.int[1]
  )
})

RMU

gbtoolbox::reliability() estimates a within-session reliability (rmu) using the posterior samples from each subject.

Retest sample (N = 115)

get_draws_matrix = function(fit, ids, par) {
  m = fit$draws(variables = par, format = "matrix") # draws x N
  colnames(m) = ids
  t(m) # N x draws
}

extract_rmu = function(fit, ids, session_label, pars = subj_pars) {
  map_dfr(pars, function(p) {
    # browser()
    rel = reliability(get_draws_matrix(fit, ids, p))
    tibble(
      parameter = p,
      method    = paste0("RMU (", session_label, ")"),
      estimate  = rel$hdci$rmu_estimate,
      se        = sd(rel$reliability_posterior_draws), # posterior SD of the RMU draws
      lower     = rel$hdci$hdci_lowerbound,
      upper     = rel$hdci$hdci_upperbound,
      width     = rel$hdci$hdci_upperbound - rel$hdci$hdci_lowerbound
    )
  })
}

rmu = bind_rows(
  extract_rmu(fit_bandit_t1, ids_t1, "T1, N = 115"),
  extract_rmu(fit_bandit_t2, ids_t2, "T2, N = 115")
)

Split-half reliability

In this section, we split the data from each timepoint/session into two equally sized halves. We then fit the models on each split-half dataset independently.

The correlation between the two split-half datasets estimates the reliability of each split-half dataset, not of the combined data. To estimate the reliability of the full-length test, the correlations are adjusted using the Spearman-Brown “prophecy” formula.

Retest sample (N = 115)

spearman_brown = function(r) 2 * r / (1 + r)

splithalf_session = function(fit_first, fit_second, ids, session_label) {
  indpars_first  = extract_indpars(fit_first,  ids)
  indpars_second = extract_indpars(fit_second, ids)
  stopifnot(identical(indpars_first$id, indpars_second$id))

  map_dfr(subj_pars, function(p) {
    ct   = cor.test(indpars_first[[p]], indpars_second[[p]])
    r    = unname(ct$estimate)
    se_r = sqrt((1 - r^2) / ct$parameter) # SE of the underlying split-half r
    tibble(
      parameter = p,
      method    = paste0("Split-Half ", session_label),
      estimate  = spearman_brown(r),
      se        = se_r * 2 / (1 + r)^2, # delta method through the Spearman-Brown transform
      lower     = spearman_brown(ct$conf.int[1]),
      upper     = spearman_brown(ct$conf.int[2]),
      width     = spearman_brown(ct$conf.int[2]) - spearman_brown(ct$conf.int[1])
    )
  })
}

splithalf = bind_rows(
  splithalf_session(fit_bandit_t1_first, fit_bandit_t1_second, ids_splithalf, "(T1, N = 115)"),
  splithalf_session(fit_bandit_t2_first, fit_bandit_t2_second, ids_splithalf, "(T2, N = 115)")
)

Appendix: the Stan model

Source

The stan model used to fit the Bayesian models is bandit4arm_4par.stan, shipped inside the hBayesDM package (system.file("stan_files", "bandit4arm_4par.stan", package = "hBayesDM")) and printed in full below:

/*
    hBayesDM is free software: you can redistribute it and/or modify
    it under the terms of the GNU General Public License as published by
    the Free Software Foundation, either version 3 of the License, or
    (at your option) any later version.

    hBayesDM is distributed in the hope that it will be useful,
    but WITHOUT ANY WARRANTY; without even the implied warranty of
    MERCHANTABILITY or FITNESS FOR A PARTICULAR PURPOSE.  See the
    GNU General Public License for more details.

    You should have received a copy of the GNU General Public License
    along with hBayesDM.  If not, see <http://www.gnu.org/licenses/>.
*/

// Seymour et al 2012 J neuro model, w/o C (chioce perseveration)
data {
  int<lower=1> N;
  int<lower=1> T;
  array[N] int<lower=1, upper=T> Tsubj;
  array[N, T] real rew;
  array[N, T] real los;
  array[N, T] int choice;
}
transformed data {
  vector[4] initV;
  initV = rep_vector(0.0, 4);
}
parameters {
  // Declare all parameters as vectors for vectorizing
  // Hyper(group)-parameters
  vector[4] mu_pr;
  vector<lower=0>[4] sigma;
  
  // Subject-level raw parameters (for Matt trick)
  vector[N] Arew_pr;
  vector[N] Apun_pr;
  vector[N] R_pr;
  vector[N] P_pr;
}
transformed parameters {
  // Transform subject-level raw parameters
  vector<lower=0, upper=1>[N] Arew;
  vector<lower=0, upper=1>[N] Apun;
  vector<lower=0, upper=30>[N] R;
  vector<lower=0, upper=30>[N] P;
  
  for (i in 1 : N) {
    Arew[i] = Phi_approx(mu_pr[1] + sigma[1] * Arew_pr[i]);
    Apun[i] = Phi_approx(mu_pr[2] + sigma[2] * Apun_pr[i]);
    R[i] = Phi_approx(mu_pr[3] + sigma[3] * R_pr[i]) * 30;
    P[i] = Phi_approx(mu_pr[4] + sigma[4] * P_pr[i]) * 30;
  }
}
model {
  // Hyperparameters
  mu_pr ~ normal(0, 1);
  sigma ~ normal(0, 0.2);
  
  // individual parameters
  Arew_pr ~ normal(0, 1.0);
  Apun_pr ~ normal(0, 1.0);
  R_pr ~ normal(0, 1.0);
  P_pr ~ normal(0, 1.0);
  
  for (i in 1 : N) {
    // Define values
    vector[4] Qr;
    vector[4] Qp;
    vector[4] PEr_fic; // prediction error - for reward fictive updating (for unchosen options)
    vector[4] PEp_fic; // prediction error - for punishment fictive updating (for unchosen options)
    vector[4] Qsum; // Qsum = Qrew + Qpun + perseverance
    
    real Qr_chosen;
    real Qp_chosen;
    real PEr; // prediction error - for reward of the chosen option
    real PEp; // prediction error - for punishment of the chosen option
    
    // Initialize values
    Qr = initV;
    Qp = initV;
    Qsum = initV;
    
    for (t in 1 : Tsubj[i]) {
      // softmax choice
      choice[i, t] ~ categorical_logit(Qsum);
      
      // Prediction error signals
      PEr = R[i] * rew[i, t] - Qr[choice[i, t]];
      PEp = P[i] * los[i, t] - Qp[choice[i, t]];
      PEr_fic = -Qr;
      PEp_fic = -Qp;
      
      // store chosen deck Q values (rew and pun)
      Qr_chosen = Qr[choice[i, t]];
      Qp_chosen = Qp[choice[i, t]];
      
      // First, update Qr & Qp for all decks w/ fictive updating
      Qr += Arew[i] * PEr_fic;
      Qp += Apun[i] * PEp_fic;
      // Replace Q values of chosen deck with correct values using stored values
      Qr[choice[i, t]] = Qr_chosen + Arew[i] * PEr;
      Qp[choice[i, t]] = Qp_chosen + Apun[i] * PEp;
      
      // Q(sum)
      Qsum = Qr + Qp;
    }
  }
}
generated quantities {
  // For group level parameters
  real<lower=0, upper=1> mu_Arew;
  real<lower=0, upper=1> mu_Apun;
  real<lower=0, upper=30> mu_R;
  real<lower=0, upper=30> mu_P;
  
  // For log likelihood calculation
  array[N] real log_lik;
  
  // For posterior predictive check
  array[N, T] real y_pred;
  
  // Set all posterior predictions to 0 (avoids NULL values)
  for (i in 1 : N) {
    for (t in 1 : T) {
      y_pred[i, t] = -1;
    }
  }
  
  mu_Arew = Phi_approx(mu_pr[1]);
  mu_Apun = Phi_approx(mu_pr[2]);
  mu_R = Phi_approx(mu_pr[3]) * 30;
  mu_P = Phi_approx(mu_pr[4]) * 30;
  
  {
    // local section, this saves time and space
    for (i in 1 : N) {
      // Define values
      vector[4] Qr;
      vector[4] Qp;
      vector[4] PEr_fic; // prediction error - for reward fictive updating (for unchosen options)
      vector[4] PEp_fic; // prediction error - for punishment fictive updating (for unchosen options)
      vector[4] Qsum; // Qsum = Qrew + Qpun + perseverance
      
      real Qr_chosen;
      real Qp_chosen;
      real PEr; // prediction error - for reward of the chosen option
      real PEp; // prediction error - for punishment of the chosen option
      
      // Initialize values
      Qr = initV;
      Qp = initV;
      Qsum = initV;
      log_lik[i] = 0.0;
      
      for (t in 1 : Tsubj[i]) {
        // compute log likelihood of current trial
        log_lik[i] += categorical_logit_lpmf(choice[i, t] | Qsum);
        
        // generate posterior prediction for current trial
        y_pred[i, t] = categorical_rng(softmax(Qsum));
        
        // Prediction error signals
        PEr = R[i] * rew[i, t] - Qr[choice[i, t]];
        PEp = P[i] * los[i, t] - Qp[choice[i, t]];
        PEr_fic = -Qr;
        PEp_fic = -Qp;
        
        // store chosen deck Q values (rew and pun)
        Qr_chosen = Qr[choice[i, t]];
        Qp_chosen = Qp[choice[i, t]];
        
        // First, update Qr & Qp for all decks w/ fictive updating
        Qr += Arew[i] * PEr_fic;
        Qp += Apun[i] * PEp_fic;
        // Replace Q values of chosen deck with correct values using stored values
        Qr[choice[i, t]] = Qr_chosen + Arew[i] * PEr;
        Qp[choice[i, t]] = Qp_chosen + Apun[i] * PEp;
        
        // Q(sum)
        Qsum = Qr + Qp;
      }
    }
  }
}

Model description

Task: A hierarchical Rescorla-Wagner learner for a 4-armed bandit, where each arm can independently deliver a reward and a punishment on the same trial (Seymour et al., 2012).

Notation: Subjects are indexed \(i = 1, \dots, N\), trials \(t = 1, \dots, T_i\) (the number of trials subject \(i\) actually completed) and arms \(k \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}\). On trial \(t\), subject \(i\) chooses arm \(c_{it} \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}\) and then observes a reward \(\text{rew}_{it} \in \{0, 1\}\) and a punishment \(\text{pun}_{it} \in \{0, -1\}\). These are the gain and loss columns built by bandit4arm_df() (see above); hBayesDM flips the sign of loss internally so that punishments enter the model as negative numbers.

Parameters: Every subject gets their own

  • \(\alpha^{r}_i\) – reward learning rate (Arew)
  • \(\alpha^{p}_i\) – punishment learning rate (Apun)
  • \(R_i\) – reward sensitivity (R), i.e. how much subject \(i\) likes reward
  • \(P_i\) – punishment sensitivity (P), i.e. how much subject \(i\) dislikes punishment

Latent values: Each subject carries two separate expectations for every arm: a reward expectation \(Q^{r}_{itk}\) and a punishment expectation \(Q^{p}_{itk}\). Choices are driven by their sum, the net value of each arm:

\[ Q^{\Sigma}_{itk} = Q^{r}_{itk} + Q^{p}_{itk} \]

Choice rule

On every trial the choice is a softmax over the four net values:

\[ c_{it} \sim \text{Categorical}\left(\pi_{it}\right), \qquad \pi_{itk} = \Pr\left(c_{it} = k\right) = \frac{\exp\left(Q^{\Sigma}_{itk}\right)}{\sum_{j=1}^{4} \exp\left(Q^{\Sigma}_{itj}\right)} \]

Note there is no separate inverse-temperature parameter: because \(R_i\) and \(P_i\) scale the magnitude of the \(Q\) values (see the prediction errors below), they also set how deterministic a subject’s choices are.

Initial values

At the start of the task all expectations are zero,

\[ Q^{r}_{i1k} = Q^{p}_{i1k} = 0 \qquad \text{for all } k, \]

so the first choice is made at random (\(\pi_{i1k} = 1/4\) for every arm).

Prediction errors for the chosen arm

After choosing arm \(c_{it}\) and observing the outcome, the subject computes a reward prediction error and a punishment prediction error for that arm only:

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{PE}^{r}_{it} &= R_i \cdot \text{rew}_{it} - Q^{r}_{i t c_{it}} \\ \text{PE}^{p}_{it} &= P_i \cdot \text{pun}_{it} - Q^{p}_{i t c_{it}} \end{aligned} \]

Each is the outcome actually received (scaled by the subject’s sensitivity) minus what was expected for the chosen arm. Scaling the raw outcome by \(R_i\) or \(P_i\) is how the model accounts for individual differences in the overall impact of rewards and punishments: a subject with a large \(R_i\) experiences a larger reward prediction error from the same win than a subject with a small \(R_i\).

Fictive prediction errors for the unchosen arms

The unchosen arms are also updated on every trial, as if they had been chosen and delivered no reward and no punishment (fictive, or counterfactual, updating). Their prediction errors are therefore the negative of the current expectation, for every arm \(k\):

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{PEF}^{r}_{itk} &= 0 - Q^{r}_{itk} \\ \text{PEF}^{p}_{itk} &= 0 - Q^{p}_{itk} \end{aligned} \]

Value updating

The expectations carried into the next trial are updated Rescorla-Wagner style, with separate learning rates for reward and punishment. For the chosen arm (\(k = c_{it}\)):

\[ \begin{aligned} Q^{r}_{i,t+1,k} &= Q^{r}_{itk} + \alpha^{r}_i \cdot \text{PE}^{r}_{it} \\ Q^{p}_{i,t+1,k} &= Q^{p}_{itk} + \alpha^{p}_i \cdot \text{PE}^{p}_{it} \end{aligned} \]

For every unchosen arm (\(k \neq c_{it}\)):

\[ \begin{aligned} Q^{r}_{i,t+1,k} &= Q^{r}_{itk} + \alpha^{r}_i \cdot \text{PEF}^{r}_{itk} = \left(1 - \alpha^{r}_i\right) Q^{r}_{itk} \\ Q^{p}_{i,t+1,k} &= Q^{p}_{itk} + \alpha^{p}_i \cdot \text{PEF}^{p}_{itk} = \left(1 - \alpha^{p}_i\right) Q^{p}_{itk} \end{aligned} \]

i.e. every unchosen arm’s reward and punishment expectations decay a fraction \(\alpha^{r}_i\) and \(\alpha^{p}_i\) of the way back toward zero on every trial. (In the Stan code the fictive update is applied to all four arms first and the chosen arm’s entry is then overwritten with the real update; the result is exactly the two cases above.)

This makes sense for the fluctuating bandit task because the reward and punishment probabilities change over time - so that prior knowledge is less useful.

Hierarchical priors (non-centred parameterisation)

All four subject-level parameters are bounded (\(\alpha^{r}_i, \alpha^{p}_i \in [0, 1]\) and \(R_i, P_i \in [0, 30]\)) but are not sampled on those scales directly. Instead each subject gets an unconstrained standard-normal score \(z_i\), the population location \(\mu\) and scale \(\sigma\) are applied on that unconstrained scale, and the result is pushed through the standard normal CDF \(\Phi(\cdot)\) (Stan’s Phi_approx(), a fast approximation) to land in \((0, 1)\), then stretched by 30 for the two sensitivities:

\[ \begin{aligned} \alpha^{r}_i &= \Phi\left(\mu_1 + \sigma_1 \, z^{r}_i\right) \\ \alpha^{p}_i &= \Phi\left(\mu_2 + \sigma_2 \, z^{p}_i\right) \\ R_i &= 30 \cdot \Phi\left(\mu_3 + \sigma_3 \, z^{R}_i\right) \\ P_i &= 30 \cdot \Phi\left(\mu_4 + \sigma_4 \, z^{P}_i\right) \end{aligned} \]

with priors

\[ \begin{aligned} z^{r}_i, \; z^{p}_i, \; z^{R}_i, \; z^{P}_i &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1) \\ \mu_j &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1) \\ \sigma_j &\sim \mathcal{N}^{+}(0, 0.2) \end{aligned} \qquad j = 1, \dots, 4 \]

\(\mu\) (mu_pr) and \(\sigma\) (sigma) are therefore the population mean and SD on the probit scale, not on the learning-rate/sensitivity scale – \(\mu_1 = 0\) means a population centred on \(\alpha^{r} = 0.5\), and to read \(\sigma\) you have to push it through \(\Phi\) too. The half-normal \(\sigma_j \sim \mathcal{N}^{+}(0, 0.2)\) is hBayesDM’s own prior for this model, the same tightened-sigma fix this project’s earlier custom model needed to hand-add for its own convergence problems.

Equation Stan Meaning
\(c_{it}\) choice[i, t] arm chosen (1-4)
\(\text{rew}_{it}\) rew[i, t] reward on that trial (gain column; 1 or 0)
\(\text{pun}_{it}\) los[i, t] punishment on that trial, -abs(loss) (0 or -1)
\(T_i\) Tsubj[i] trials completed by subject \(i\)
\(Q^{r}_{it \cdot}\), \(Q^{p}_{it \cdot}\), \(Q^{\Sigma}_{it \cdot}\) Qr, Qp, Qsum reward / punishment / net expectations, all four arms
\(\text{PE}^{r}_{it}\), \(\text{PE}^{p}_{it}\) PEr, PEp prediction errors, chosen arm
\(\text{PEF}^{r}_{it \cdot}\), \(\text{PEF}^{p}_{it \cdot}\) PEr_fic, PEp_fic fictive prediction errors, all four arms
\(\alpha^{r}_i\), \(\alpha^{p}_i\) Arew[i], Apun[i] reward / punishment learning rates
\(R_i\), \(P_i\) R[i], P[i] reward / punishment sensitivities
\(z^{r}_i\), \(z^{p}_i\), \(z^{R}_i\), \(z^{P}_i\) Arew_pr[i], Apun_pr[i], R_pr[i], P_pr[i] subject-level standard-normal scores
\(\mu_j\), \(\sigma_j\) mu_pr[j], sigma[j] population mean / SD on the probit scale
